Original Research


The Effect of the Number of Carries
on Injury Risk and Subsequent Season’s
Performance Among Running Backs in the
National Football League
Matthew J. Kraeutler,*† MD, John W. Belk,† and Eric C. McCarty,† MD
Investigation performed at CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center, University of Colorado
School of Medicine, Department of Orthopedics, Boulder, Colorado, USA

Background: In recent years, several studies have correlated pitch count with an increased risk for injury among baseball pitchers.
However, no studies have attempted to draw a similar conclusion based on number of carries by running backs (RBs) in football.
Purpose: To determine whether there is a correlation between number of carries by RBs in the National Football League (NFL) and
risk of injury or worsened performance in the subsequent season.
Study Design: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: The ESPN NFL statistics archives were searched from the 2004 through 2014 regular seasons. During each season, data
were collected on RBs with 150 to 250 carries (group A) and 300þ carries (group B). The following data were collected for each
player and compared between groups: number of carries and mean yards per carry during the regular season of interest and the
subsequent season, number of games missed due to injury during the season of interest and the subsequent season, and the
specific injuries resulting in missed playing time during the subsequent season. Matched-pair t tests were used to compare
changes within each group from one season to the next in terms of number of carries, mean yards per carry, and games missed
due to injury.
Results: During the seasons studied, a total of 275 RBs were included (group A, 212; group B, 63). In group A, 140 RBs (66%)
missed at least 1 game the subsequent season due to injury, compared with 31 RBs (49%) in group B (P ¼ .016). In fact, players in
group B missed significantly fewer games due to injury during the season of interest (P < .0001) as well as the subsequent season
(P < .01). Mean yards per carry was not significantly different between groups in the preceding season (P ¼ .073) or the subsequent
season (P ¼ .24).
Conclusion: NFL RBs with a high number of carries are not placed at greater risk of injury or worsened performance during the
subsequent season. These RBs may be generally less injury prone compared with other NFL RBs.
Keywords: National Football League; running back; injury

13	      Clinical Scenario: Cryotherapy is one of the most commonly used modalities for postexercise muscle recovery despite
14	      inconsistencies in the literature validating its effectiveness. With the need to ﬁnd a more effective modality, photobiomodula-
15	      tion therapy (PBMT) has gained popularity because of recent research demonstrating its ability to accelerate the muscle
16	      recovery process. Focused Clinical Question: Is PBMT more effective than cryotherapy at reducing recovery time and
17	      decreasing delayed onset muscle soreness after strenuous exercise? Summary of Key Findings: Three moderate- to high-
18	      quality double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trials and 2 low- to moderate-quality translational studies performed
19	      on rats were included in this critically appraised topic. All 5 studies supported the use of PBMT over cryotherapy as a
20	      treatment for postexercise muscle recovery following exercise. PBMT was superior in reducing creatine kinase, inﬂammation
21	      markers, and blood lactate compared with cryotherapy, following strenuous/high intensity aerobic or strength muscular
22	      exercise. PBMT was also shown to improve postexercise muscle performance and function more than cryotherapy. Clinical
23	      Bottom Line: There is moderate evidence to suggest the use of PBMT over cryotherapy postexercise to enhance muscle
24	      recovery in trained and untrained athletes. Shorter recovery times and increased muscle performance can be seen 24 to
25	      96 hours following PBMT application. Strength of Recommendation: Based on consistent ﬁndings from all 5 studies, there is
26	      grade B evidence to support the use of PBMT over cryotherapy for more effective postexercise recovery of skeletal muscle
27	      performance.

      Clinical Scenario: Cryotherapy is one of the most commonly used modalities for postexercise muscle recovery despite
      inconsistencies in the literature validating its effectiveness. With the need to ﬁnd a more effective modality, photobiomodula-
      tion therapy (PBMT) has gained popularity because of recent research demonstrating its ability to accelerate the muscle
      recovery process. Focused Clinical Question: Is PBMT more effective than cryotherapy at reducing recovery time and
      decreasing delayed onset muscle soreness after strenuous exercise? Summary of Key Findings: Three moderate- to high-
      quality double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trials and 2 low- to moderate-quality translational studies performed
      on rats were included in this critically appraised topic. All 5 studies supported the use of PBMT over cryotherapy as a
      treatment for postexercise muscle recovery following exercise. PBMT was superior in reducing creatine kinase, inﬂammation
      markers, and blood lactate compared with cryotherapy, following strenuous/high intensity aerobic or strength muscular
      exercise. PBMT was also shown to improve postexercise muscle performance and function more than cryotherapy. Clinical
      Bottom Line: There is moderate evidence to suggest the use of PBMT over cryotherapy postexercise to enhance muscle
      recovery in trained and untrained athletes. Shorter recovery times and increased muscle performance can be seen 24 to
      96 hours following PBMT application. Strength of Recommendation: Based on consistent ﬁndings from all 5 studies, there is
      grade B evidence to support the use of PBMT over cryotherapy for more effective postexercise recovery of skeletal muscle
      performance.

      Keywords: laser therapy, light therapy, cold therapy, cold-water immersion therapy, post-exercise

1	Review
2	The Efficacy of Nutritional Strategies and Ergogenic Aids on
3	Acute Responses and Chronic Adaptations to Exertional-Heat
4	Exposure: A Narrative Review
5	Ryan A. Dunn 1 , Grant M. Tinsley 1 , Ty B. Palmer 1 , Courteney L. Benjamin 2                            and Yasuki Sekiguchi 1, *
6	
7	                                         1   Department of Kinesiology and Sport Management, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX 79409, USA;
8	                                             dun77277@ttu.edu (R.A.D.); grant.tinsley@ttu.edu (G.M.T.); ty.palmer@ttu.edu (T.B.P.)
9	                                         2   Department of Kinesiology, Samford University, Birmingham, AL 35229, USA; cbenjami@samford.edu
10	                                         *   Correspondence: yasuki.sekiguchi@ttu.edu
11	
12	
13	                                         Abstract: Global warming is attributed to an increased frequency of high ambient temperatures and
14	                                         humidity, elevating the prevalence of high-temperature-related illness and death. Evidence over
15	                                         recent decades highlights that tailored nutritional strategies are essential to improve performance
16	                                         and optimise health during acute and chronic exertional-heat exposure. Therefore, the purpose of
17	                                         this review is to discuss the efficacy of various nutritional strategies and ergogenic aids on responses
18	                                         during and following acute and chronic exertional-heat exposure. An outline is provided surround-
19	                                         ing the application of various nutritional practices (e.g., carbohydrate loading, fluid replacement
20	                                         strategies) and ergogenic aids (e.g., caffeine, creatine, nitrate, tyrosine) to improve physiological,
21	                                         cognitive, and recovery responses to acute exertional-heat exposure. Additionally, this review will
22	                                         evaluate if the magnitude and time course of chronic heat adaptations can be modified with tai-
23	                                         lored supplementation practices. This review highlights that there is robust evidence for the use
24	                                         of certain ergogenic aids and nutritional strategies to improve performance and health outcomes
25	                                         during exertional-heat exposure. However, equivocal findings across studies appear dependent on
26	                                         factors such as exercise testing modality, duration, and intensity; outcome measures in relation to
27	                                         the ergogenic aid’s proposed mechanism of action; and sex-specific responses. Collectively, this
28	Citation: Dunn, R.A.; Tinsley, G.M.;
29	                                         review provides evidence-based recommendations and highlights areas for future research that
30	Palmer, T.B.; Benjamin, C.L.;
31	                                         have the potential to assist with prescribing specific nutritional strategies and ergogenic aids in
32	Sekiguchi, Y. The Efficacy of
33	                                         populations frequently exercising in the heat. Future research is required to establish dose-, sex-, and
34	Nutritional Strategies and Ergogenic
35	                                         exercise-modality-specific responses to various nutritional practices and ergogenic aid use for acute
36	Aids on Acute Responses and Chronic
37	Adaptations to Exertional-Heat
38	                                         and chronic exertional-heat exposure.
39	Exposure: A Narrative Review.
40	Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792. https://       Keywords: exercise; heat acclimation; heat stress; hydration; nutrition; supplement; thermoregulation
41	doi.org/10.3390/nu16223792
42	
43	Academic Editor: Jay R. Hoffman
44	
45	Received: 1 October 2024                 1. Introduction
46	Revised: 28 October 2024                       Global warming is associated with an increased frequency of high ambient temper-
47	Accepted: 2 November 2024                atures and humidity levels [1], elevating incidences of high-temperature-related illness
48	Published: 5 November 2024
49	                                         and death [2]. The addition of heightened relative humidity levels to already hot environ-
50	                                         ments causes particular challenges to overall heat storage, as reduced evaporative sweat
51	                                         losses result in a lower magnitude of heat dissipation [1,2]. In combination with elite sport
52	Copyright: © 2024 by the authors.
53	                                         globalisation, higher temperatures worldwide and associated exertional-heat stress com-
54	Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland.       promises exercise performance [3]. This includes aspects such as physical, technical/skill-
55	This article is an open access article   based, neuromuscular, and cognitive performance [4,5]. Additionally, military training
56	distributed under the terms and          and deployment often involves prolonged, intense activity in environmental extremes, fre-
57	conditions of the Creative Commons       quently undertaken with insufficient heat preparation [6,7]. Occupational thermal exposure
58	Attribution (CC BY) license (https://    (e.g., firefighting) also reduces work capacity and increases injury risk [8]. Collectively, ex-
59	creativecommons.org/licenses/by/         ercise in hot and/or humid environments exacerbates physiological and thermoregulatory
60	4.0/).                                   strain, increasing susceptibility to exertional-heat illness/stroke (EHI/EHS) [9]. This can be
61	
62	
63	
64	Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16223792                                            https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nutrients
65	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                             2 of 25
66	
67	
68	
69	                           particularly problematic for cardiovascular function when performing physical activities in
70	                           the heat, in addition to exacerbating complications arising from various common health
71	                           conditions (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes). Despite difficulties quantifying the
72	                           prevalence of EHI/EHS due to inconsistencies in terminology and criteria for diagnosis,
73	                           endurance sports and military populations experience the highest rates of heat-related
74	                           illnesses globally, with ~674.0 cases of EHI per 10,000 athlete-exposures [10]. Therefore,
75	                           exercise performance in the heat can be suboptimal, with tailored heat mitigation and
76	                           nutritional strategies required to attenuate heat-mediated decrements in performance and
77	                           health [3].
78	                                 Heat mitigation strategies such as heat acclimation/acclimatisation (HA/HAs) lessen
79	                           the magnitude of physiological, thermoregulatory, and perceptual strain associated with
80	                           exertional-heat stress [11,12]. These include body fluid and electrolyte losses, increased
81	                           core temperature (Tc ) and heart rate (HR), augmented substrate utilisation, and enhanced
82	                           thermal discomfort [13,14]. HA/HAs (involving artificial or natural heat exposures, respect-
83	                           fully) deliver regular and controlled disturbances to thermal homeostasis [11], inducing
84	                           chemical, functional, and genetic adaptations that contribute to attaining a thermotoler-
85	                           ant phenotype [12]. Collectively, these adaptations have been shown to benefit exercise
86	                           performance in the heat by reducing physiological, thermoregulatory, and cellular stress
87	                           responses during future exertional-heat exposures [9].
88	                                 Although chronic heat adaptation strategies procure the most robust adaptations
89	                           for optimal performance in the heat, singular heat exposure bouts may also improve
90	                           some aspects of exercise performance in a timelier manner [15]. Acute heat stress typically
91	                           hinders exercise performance by augmenting Tc , HR, and substrate utilisation [16]. Despite
92	                           this, Ball [17] highlights the positive implications of acute heat exposure, where elevated
93	                           muscle temperature-related improvements in metabolic and contractile functioning increase
94	                           adenosine triphosphate (ATP) turnover rates. Although the effects of acute heat exposure
95	                           on exercise performance likely depend on the modality, duration, and metabolic demand
96	                           of exercise, a bout of muscle-damaging exercise in the heat was attributed to reduced
97	                           physiological strain during future exertional-heat stress [18,19]. Additionally, heat shock
98	                           protein 70/72 expression was diminished prior to and following subsequent exertional-heat
99	                           stress, indicative of a lower magnitude of heat-induced cellular stress [20]. This highlights
100	                           the potential for acute heat exposure strategies to assist in the acquisition of a thermotolerant
101	                           phenotype [18–20]. Taken together, tailored acute and chronic heat adaptation methods
102	                           can potentially enhance exercise performance in the heat. However, it is important to
103	                           continually develop, evolve, and review these strategies with the aim of maximising
104	                           adaptation potential [21].
105	                                 Emerging evidence indicates that nutritional and hydration strategies should com-
106	                           plement heat adaptation interventions to enhance overall performance and safety under
107	                           exertional-heat stress [22]. Therefore, it is important to review the current evidence sur-
108	                           rounding these strategies to establish the efficacy and practicality of their use for exercise
109	                           in the heat [23]. Current reviews, global position stands, and consensus statements re-
110	                           garding nutritional practices to assist with exertional-heat stress have focused on athletes’
111	                           knowledge and use of heat adaptation and nutritional interventions, fluid and electrolyte re-
112	                           placement strategies for health and performance, and recovery following heat stress [22–25].
113	                           However, there is a need to evaluate the effectiveness and application of nutritional strate-
114	                           gies and ergogenic aids for various exercise settings in the heat. Therefore, the purpose of
115	                           this narrative review is to (1) discuss how different nutritional practices and ergogenic aids
116	                           influence responses to acute exertional-heat stress, and (2) discover how adaptations from
117	                           chronic heat mitigation strategies (e.g., HA/HAs) can be accelerated with the addition of
118	                           modified nutritional interventions.
119	
120	                           2. Search Strategy
121	                                All studies investigating the efficacy of various nutritional strategies and ergogenic
122	                           aids on acute responses and chronic adaptations to exertional-heat exposure were searched
123	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                               3 of 25
124	
125	
126	
127	                            through April 2024 in PubMed, SPORTDiscus™, Scopus, and Google Scholar. The key-
128	                           words used included ‘heat stress’, ‘heat acclimation’, ‘acclimatisation’, ‘thermoregulation’,
129	                           ‘endurance’, ‘neuromuscular performance’, ‘aerobic performance’, ‘intermittent sports’,
130	                           ‘team sports’, ‘exercise’, ‘diet*’, ‘ergogenic aid’, ‘supplement’, ‘nutrition’, ‘metabolism’, ‘oxi-
131	                            dation’, ‘carbohydrate’, ‘energy availability’, ‘gastrointestinal function’, ‘immune function’,
132	                           ‘adaptation’, ‘protein’, ‘recovery’, and ‘hydration.’ Subject headings were used indepen-
133	                            dently and in combination. Initial article searching was restricted to full-text articles using
134	                            human participants, published in English-language, peer-reviewed journals. Randomised
135	                            control trials, observational, crossover, and interventional studies were included for re-
136	                           view. Review articles, abstracts, case studies, unpublished theses, conference papers, and
137	                            editorials were not included for discussion. The ambient temperature of exercise perfor-
138	                            mance conditions had to exceed 28 ◦ C, simulating predicted environmental temperatures
139	                            of major sporting events [3]. Additionally, studies incorporating HA/HAs interventions
140	                           were performed for ≥5 days, representing typical short-term protocols, with a minimum of
141	                            ≥3 heat exposure sessions conducted per week. Lastly, the induction of HA/HAs-induced
142	                            adaptations had to be quantified in terms of exposure and duration, with outcome variables
143	                            measured at least pre- and immediately post-intervention (within 24 h).
144	
145	                           3. Hydration and Fluid Replacement
146	                           3.1. Hydration Status and Exertional-Heat Stress
147	                                Exertional-heat stress presents numerous challenges for health and performance.
148	                           In relation to hydration status, exercise in the heat elevates metabolic heat production,
149	                           whereby increases in sweat rate maintain thermal homeostasis via evaporative fluid losses
150	                           from the skin [26]. If fluid losses are not sufficiently replaced, reductions in total body
151	                           water and plasma volume (PV ) adversely alter cutaneous blood flow, elevate Tc , and
152	                           exacerbate cardiovascular responses during exercise [27,28]. Ultimately, this decreases
153	                           exercise capacity and compromises cardiovascular stability, increasing the susceptibility to
154	                           EHI/EHS [29]. It is generally accepted that performance impairments occur when fluid
155	                           losses exceed 2% of body mass [30]. This can be measured by recording the difference
156	                           between pre- and post-exercise body weight. Additionally, individuals can use urine colour
157	                           as simple and practical means of evaluating hydration status, with dark coloured urine
158	                           indicative of potential dehydration. Therefore, specific fluid replacement strategies are
159	                           essential to commence exercise in a euhydrated state, especially when performed in hot
160	                           and/or humid environments [31].
161	
162	                           3.2. Electrolyte Balance and Sodium Loading
163	                                 Sodium is an essential electrolyte for maintaining fluid and blood volume. However,
164	                           the majority of commercially available sports beverages contain sodium concentrations
165	                           that do not match sweat electrolyte losses from exercise, resulting in a negative sodium
166	                           balance [32]. This was initially demonstrated by Vrijens and Rehrer [33], who showed that
167	                           the ingestion of a sodium-containing sports beverage decreased plasma sodium and PV
168	                           relative to pre-exercise following a prolonged, moderate-intensity cycle in the heat (Table 1).
169	                           The purpose of the lower sodium content in sports beverages is to promote adequate
170	                           gastric emptying rates, increase beverage palatability, and favour exogenous carbohydrate
171	                           ingestion, with the aim of delaying glycogen store utilisation [31]. Regardless, most research
172	                           investigating the efficacy of sodium suggests that it has a direct role in the maintenance
173	                           and restoration of fluid and electrolyte balance during acute bouts of prolonged, moderate-
174	                           intensity exercise in the heat, and can minimise associated PV reductions when given the
175	                           appropriate dose [34,35]. Despite this, the optimal sodium dose to augment performance
176	                           and health outcomes has yet to be determined.
177	                                 The magnitude of sodium supplementation required to optimise an acute bout of
178	                           exercise in the heat is likely dependent on factors such as individual body mass, in addition
179	                           to exercise modality, duration, and intensity [32]. Hamouti and colleagues [36] identified
180	                           that water combined with moderate and high levels of sodium (82 and 164 mmol, respec-
181	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                          4 of 25
182	
183	
184	
185	                           tively) enhanced PV by ~5%, compared to ingesting water only, during prolonged exercise
186	                           in the heat. This expansion in PV allowed for the maintenance of cardiac output and stroke
187	                           volume during exercise, which in turn, led to a 7.4% improvement in cycling power output
188	                           during a time-trial in the heat [36]. This highlights the potential of appropriate sodium
189	                           ingestion for providing cardiovascular stability during exertional-heat stress [36].
190	                                Ingesting high quantities of sodium prior to an acute bout of exercise in the heat
191	                           (sodium loading) has been suggested as an effective strategy to optimise performance and
192	                           thermoregulation [37,38]. To test this hypothesis, previous research assessed the effects
193	                           of consuming 20–40 mg·kg−1 of sodium, 1–2 hrs prior to prolonged exercise in the heat
194	                           (Table 1 [36,39,40]). This research demonstrated improvements in thermoregulatory re-
195	                           sponses (lower Tc , increased sweat rate and PV ) [36,39], with acute sodium loading found to
196	                           be equally or more effective than supplementation over consecutive days [37]. Thus, acute
197	                           sodium loading may be practically beneficial for those with limited opportunities to ingest
198	                           adequate sodium concentrations prior to and during exercise in the heat. Although the
199	                           mechanisms underlying sex-specific responses to sodium consumption are not fully eluci-
200	                           dated, it should be highlighted that females may better maintain sodium balance compared
201	                           to males, likely due to heightened sodium sensitivity [38]. Thus, findings related to sodium
202	                           ingestion for exertional-heat stress in males should in theory extend to female populations,
203	                           who may potentially exhibit greater benefits due to enhanced sodium sensitivity [38]. Fu-
204	                           ture research should seek to investigate the dose–response relationship of sodium intake, in
205	                           addition to sex differences, on physiological and cognitive performance measures during
206	                           exertional-heat stress.
207	
208	                           3.3. Chronic Heat Adaptation with Permissive Dehydration
209	                                Beneficial changes induced by chronic heat adaptation strategies may be influenced
210	                           by the hydration strategy adopted (i.e., maintained euhydration or dehydration via fluid
211	                           restriction) [12,41]. Commencing repeated HA sessions in a dehydrated state (fluid loss
212	                           of ~2–3% of body mass), termed permissive dehydration, may accelerate physiological
213	                           adaptations due to the interrelationship between heat strain and dehydration [42]. HA
214	                           undertaken with permissive dehydration can increase plasma vasopressin and aldosterone
215	                           concentrations, attributed to improved renal water retention and regulation of blood pres-
216	                           sure during exertional-heat stress [43,44]. Furthermore, research showed that permissive
217	                           dehydration during a short-term HA protocol (5 days) in trained athletes increased sweat
218	                           rate and electrolyte retention, expanded PV , and augmented cardiovascular and thermoreg-
219	                           ulatory adaptations compared to HA sessions with euhydration [45]. These findings have
220	                           direct implications for HA prescription in exercise settings, with a possible means of accel-
221	                           erating adaptation time course and lessening the time burden associated with chronic heat
222	                           adaptation protocols [11].
223	                                Despite potential positive implications of HA with permissive dehydration, athletes
224	                           and their support teams should be cautious when adopting this strategy, as purposely
225	                           being dehydrated prior to exercise in the heat can exacerbate EHI/EHS risk. Further-
226	                           more, research surrounding HA with permissive dehydration is equivocal, whereby Neal
227	                           and colleagues [46] concluded that it did not produce superior adaptations compared to
228	                           sessions conducted with euhydration (Table 1). Likewise, Travers et al. [47] highlighted
229	                           that HA significantly improved power output during time-trial performance in the heat
230	                           when sessions were conducted in a euhydrated state (+19 ± 16 Watts; p = 0.02), with
231	                           exercise performance adaptations diminished when HA sessions were performed with
232	                           permissive dehydration [47]. Additionally, when thermal strain is matched, the time course
233	                           and magnitude of HA-induced adaptations are largely unaffected by permissive dehy-
234	                           dration, compared to maintaining euhydration [47]. From a health perspective, chronic
235	                           exertional-heat stress with dehydration may be a contributing factor to acute kidney infec-
236	                           tion and potential chronic kidney disease [47]. The only study to investigate this showed
237	                           that HA with permissive dehydration offered no further benefit to exercise performance or
238	                           physiological adaptations; however, no increases in acute kidney infection markers were
239	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                             5 of 25
240	
241	
242	
243	                           demonstrated [48]. Collectively, current evidence regarding the effectiveness of commenc-
244	                           ing HA sessions in a dehydrated state is equivocal and likely to be highly individualised.
245	                           Additionally, further research is required to assess the true effect of this strategy on markers
246	                           of kidney function and overall health.
247	
248	                           4. Carbohydrates
249	                           4.1. Substrate Utilisation During Exercise in the Heat
250	                                 During exertional-heat stress, there is an increased reliance on muscle glycogen and
251	                           anaerobic metabolism [49], which can deplete endogenous glycogen stores quicker than
252	                           exercise in temperate climates. As such, carbohydrate intake strategies become increasingly
253	                           important in line with the elevated magnitude of heat stress and heightened substrate
254	                           utilisation rates. It should also be highlighted that males are proposed to expend more
255	                           energy from carbohydrate sources during prolonged exercise in comparison to females
256	                           (53.1% vs. 45.7% [50]). This is likely due to their higher respiratory exchange ratio and
257	                           emphasises the importance of appropriate carbohydrate intake prior to and during exer-
258	                           cise [50]. Individuals exercising for ≥90 min are recommended to consume 30–90 g·h−1 of
259	                           carbohydrates to maintain blood glucose levels during exercise. Such maintenance may
260	                           help delay the onset of fatigue and increase exercise capacity in the heat, particularly in
261	                           male populations [51].
262	
263	                           4.2. Intestinal Permeability and Exogenous Carbohydrate Consumption
264	                                Exertional-heat stress also compromises intestinal wall integrity, resulting in detrimen-
265	                           tal downstream signalling cascades which elicit gastrointestinal disturbances, or in more
266	                           severe cases, EHI/EHS [52,53]. For example, increases in Tc as minimal as 1.3 ◦ C have
267	                           produced elevations in intestinal permeability and secretions of endotoxins that exacerbate
268	                           pro-inflammatory immune responses [54]. Exogenous carbohydrates may protect against
269	                           intestinal permeability, where increased production of short-chain fatty acids induce the
270	                           formation of plaque and membrane proteins that enhance epithelial barrier integrity [54].
271	                           In relation, Snipe and colleagues [55] highlighted that ad libitum carbohydrate ingestion
272	                           during 120 min of submaximal exercise in the heat (60% maximal oxygen uptake [VO2max ])
273	                           ameliorated intestinal epithelial injury, small intestine permeability, and enhanced anti-
274	                           endotoxin antibody responses when compared to water ingestion alone. Additionally,
275	                           30–90 g·h−1 of carbohydrates can attenuate pro-inflammatory cytokine production dur-
276	                           ing exercise, indicative of reduced oxidative stress and inflammatory markers [56]. Taken
277	                           together, it appears that carbohydrate intake during exercise in the heat is important for low-
278	                           ering glycogen depletion rates, and has direct implications for reducing the susceptibility
279	                           of EHI/EHS, primarily via intestinal protective mechanisms [54].
280	                                With most nutritional strategies, the appropriate method and dosage of supplemen-
281	                           tation is essential to provide the desired effect. Of note, Sessions and colleagues [57]
282	                           demonstrated that 26 g of carbohydrate ingestion during exercise in the heat enhanced
283	                           markers of gastrointestinal wall damage, which may exacerbate EHI/EHS symptoms
284	                           (Table 1). However, carbohydrates were administered via gels, which may indicate that
285	                           more concentrated ingestion methods alter gastrointestinal function to a higher extent than
286	                           diluted carbohydrate sources (e.g., carbohydrate containing beverages) [57]. Ultimately,
287	                           carbohydrate supplementation should be closely monitored during training/practice ses-
288	                           sions in the heat to assess the efficacy of their use on markers of gastrointestinal distress
289	                           and performance [51].
290	
291	                           4.3. Carbohydrate Loading for Exercise in the Heat
292	                                Carbohydrate-loading strategies are often implemented to maximise muscle and liver
293	                           glycogen availability prior to prolonged endurance exercise. Individuals are recommended
294	                           to consume 10–12 g·kg−1 of carbohydrates, 36–48 h before competition [58,59]. During
295	                           exercise in the heat, redistribution of blood flow to the skin from vital organs and elevations
296	                           in muscle temperature promoting glycogenolysis likely reduce exogenous carbohydrate
297	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                            6 of 25
298	
299	
300	
301	                           utilisation rates [60]. This highlights the importance of adequate carbohydrate intake prior
302	                           to exercise in the heat. It is yet to be determined if HA/HAs play a role in ameliorating heat-
303	                           mediated reductions in exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates [60]. However, combining
304	                           glucose- and fructose-based carbohydrates (i.e., multiple transportable carbohydrates)
305	                           promotes higher exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates than glucose ingestion alone [61].
306	                           Therefore, individuals are recommended to ingest combined carbohydrate sources to
307	                           maximise oxidation rates and extend exercise capacity in the heat [61].
308	
309	                           4.4. Carbohydrate Periodisation and Exertional-Heat Stress
310	                                 In contrast to carbohydrate loading, periodisation strategies, such as training with low
311	                           carbohydrate availability, are employed to increase the efficiency of utilising available fuel
312	                           sources during exercise [62,63]. Training with low carbohydrate availability potentially
313	                           enhances fat oxidation rates and skeletal muscle signalling, which have been attributed to
314	                           improvements in endurance running in both sexes [64]. As exercise in the heat increases
315	                           carbohydrate metabolism rates, the combined effect of exertional-heat stress and low
316	                           carbohydrate availability may alleviate reductions in carbohydrate oxidation rates [65].
317	                           As such, Bennett and colleagues [66] investigated the potential role of exertional-heat stress
318	                           and low carbohydrate availability on optimising substrate metabolism during exercise.
319	                           The authors identified that under exertional-heat stress, endurance training completed
320	                           with low carbohydrate availability did not improve performance in hot or temperate
321	                           conditions and failed to increase fat oxidation rates in males [66]. It is yet to be determined
322	                           if these findings will also extend to females, who are suggested to have higher relative fat
323	                           oxidation rates than males during exercise [54]. Although exercising with low carbohydrate
324	                           availability has exhibited positive benefits in temperate conditions, it appears that this
325	                           strategy requires further study to provide a rationale for its use during exercise in the
326	                           heat [54].
327	
328	                           5. Protein
329	                           5.1. Protein and Carbohydrate Supplementation and Exercise Performance
330	                                Despite not being directly related to one another in terms of their function within the
331	                           body, there is growing interest surrounding the additive use of protein to carbohydrates
332	                           (CHO + PRO) to further augment exercise performance [67]. Initial research assessed
333	                           whether combined carbohydrate and protein supplementation (CHO, 3.6 kcals·kg−1 ; PRO,
334	                           0.36 g·kg−1 ) during a 5-day aerobic training protocol in a thermoneutral environment
335	                           could enhance physiological and thermoregulatory adaptations [68]. The authors identi-
336	                           fied that consuming CHO + PRO expanded PV two-fold higher and reduced Tc , which
337	                           was associated with reduced thermoregulatory and cardiovascular strain during future
338	                           exertional-heat stress [68]. Increases in PV were attributed to elevated plasma albumin
339	                           content, subsequently enhancing plasma oncotic pressure to move fluid from the extra- to
340	                           intravascular space [68]. These findings support the potential for integrating CHO + PRO
341	                           supplementation during HA/HAs sessions to enhance cardiovascular and thermoregula-
342	                           tory adaptations.
343	                                Combined CHO + PRO supplementation may also be an effective nutritional strategy
344	                           for exertional-heat stress. Cathcart and colleagues [67] demonstrated that CHO + PRO
345	                           ingestion (PRO, 18 g·L−1 ; CHO, 76 g·L−1 ) helped maintain individual body mass during
346	                           a prolonged, multi-day cycling competition in the heat compared to consuming carbohy-
347	                           drates alone. The combination of carbohydrates and protein may mitigate the negative
348	                           effects of dehydration and associated body mass loss [67]. Additionally, Cathcart et al. [67]
349	                           found an attenuated rise in tympanic temperature, with athletes completing the race 12%
350	                           more quickly than those supplementing with only carbohydrates (Table 1 [67]). This was
351	                           the first study to assess the ergogenic benefits of CHO + PRO ingestion on prolonged
352	                           exercise in the heat [67]. However, this study’s mitigation of body mass loss may, in part,
353	                           be due to an increased caloric delivery during exercise resulting from additional protein,
354	                           with a potential protein-mediated expansion of body water compartments [69].
355	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                          7 of 25
356	
357	
358	
359	                                 Currently, studies reporting an ergogenic effect with CHO + PRO supplementation
360	                           during exercise in the heat have typically involved conditions where carbohydrate delivery
361	                           was suboptimal [70]. When carbohydrate delivery is ≥60 g·h−1 , the addition of protein has
362	                           shown no ergogenic advantage during time-to-exhaustion [71] or time-trial performance
363	                           tests [72]. Consequently, a lack of robust evidence exists to support the additive use of
364	                           protein to exogenous carbohydrates for enhancing endurance exercise performance when
365	                           carbohydrate delivery is optimal [73–75]. Additionally, most studies reporting exercise per-
366	                           formance improvements have used beverages matched for carbohydrate content, but not
367	                           total energy content, making it unclear whether benefits stemmed from protein-stimulated
368	                           mechanisms or from extra energy content within the CHO + PRO beverage [76]. Addi-
369	                           tionally, there is a lack of consideration of the potential influence of female hormonal
370	                           fluctuations on muscle protein synthesis, whereby changes in ovarian hormones have
371	                           the potential to inhibit muscle protein synthesis [67]. This is a particular concern for the
372	                           maintenance of body mass and muscle recovery throughout exertional-heat stress [67].
373	                           Taken together, differing methodologies across studies, including experimental design,
374	                           exercise performance measures, alterations in hormone secretion, and whether control
375	                           groups were matched for caloric or carbohydrate content, are likely to account for the
376	                           equivocal findings on CHO + PRO supplementation across the literature.
377	
378	                           5.2. Protein and Carbohydrate Supplementation for Recovery Following Exertional-Heat Stress
379	                                 Although CHO + PRO ingestion warrants further investigation to fully elucidate
380	                           its role in eliciting physiological and performance adaptations during acute and chronic
381	                           heat exposure, this strategy may exert the most beneficial effect on exertional-heat stress
382	                           recovery [77]. Several studies demonstrated either increased muscle glycogen restora-
383	                           tion mediated by augmented insulin concentration [77–79] or reduced markers of muscle
384	                           damage [74,80–83] when CHO + PRO is ingested during or following exercise in the heat
385	                           compared to CHO alone. The co-ingestion of CHO + PRO likely exerts positive influences
386	                           on net protein balance via increased protein synthesis and reduced protein degradation,
387	                           which may be particularly important for females experiencing reductions in muscle protein
388	                           synthesis due to ovarian hormone fluctuations during their menstrual cycle [84]. Fur-
389	                           thermore, exogenous carbohydrates stimulate the release of insulin, which has previously
390	                           been shown to enhance muscle protein synthesis and muscle fibre repair [81]. Hall and
391	                           colleagues [85] identified that CHO + PRO consumption (PRO, 0.23 g·kg−1 ·hr−1 ; CHO,
392	                           0.87 g·kg−1 ·hr−1 ) during a 2.5 h, high-intensity training session elicited a 1.8% improve-
393	                           ment in subsequent cycling time-trial performance in the heat (compared to carbohydrates
394	                           alone) following a 4 h recovery period. CHO + PRO ingestion was also associated with
395	                           significant reductions in HR, perceived exertion, and markers of muscle damage, indi-
396	                           cating a potential role in reducing physiological and perceptual stress measures during
397	                           exertional-heat stress, in addition to accelerating muscle recovery [85].
398	                                 Due to conflicting results, current evidence suggesting that CHO + PRO ingestion can
399	                           enhance exercise performance is unclear. Despite this, as exertional-heat stress exacerbates
400	                           carbohydrate utilisation, combining carbohydrates with protein may be more beneficial
401	                           for exercise in the heat, as optimal carbohydrate oxidation rates are likely more difficult
402	                           to achieve [85]. Additionally, CHO + PRO ingestion has been shown to improve exercise
403	                           recovery in both sexes without negatively influencing performance. Therefore, CHO + PRO
404	                           may be a beneficial strategy for recovery during and following exertional-heat stress.
405	                           In accordance with established guidelines, male and female athletes are recommended to
406	                           consume 1.4–2.0 g·kg−1 of protein daily, with an optimal protein dose of 20–40 g every
407	                           3–4 h to facilitate muscle protein synthesis and optimise recovery [86].

488	                           6. Caffeine
489	                           6.1. Mechanism of Action
490	                                During exercise, increased physiological strain causes disturbances to normal central
491	                           nervous system (CNS) function [87], likely resulting from an imbalance in neurotransmitters.
492	                           These effects are increasingly worsened with elevations in ambient temperature and/or
493	                           humidity [88]. To counteract the deleterious effects of exertional-heat stress on the CNS,
494	                           caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) supplementation may be beneficial [89]. The application
495	                           of caffeine on exercise performance in temperate conditions has been extensively studied;
496	                           however, data regarding caffeine’s ergogenic effect on exercise performance in the heat
497	                           are limited and inconsistent [90]. Although the precise mechanism by which caffeine
498	                           acts to enhance exercise performance is not fully elucidated, evidence suggests that a
499	                           blockage of adenosine receptors in the CNS delays the onset of central fatigue during
500	                           exercise via reductions in the inhibitory effects of adenosine on neuroexcitability and
501	                           neurotransmitter release [91]. An increase in adenosine binding to its receptors acts as a CNS
502	                           depressant, leading individuals to feel heightened sensations of sleepiness and reduced
503	                           arousal [91]. Therefore, caffeine consumption has the potential to increase motivation, drive,
504	                           and alertness, in addition to lowering perceived exertion during exercise, and enhancing
505	                           the mobilisation of intracellular calcium and free fatty acids [92]. Collectively, caffeine
506	                           ingestion may positively influence neuromuscular and cognitive performance measures via
507	                           reductions in central fatigue development (failure to sustain CNS drive to working muscle),
508	                           subsequently improving exercise tolerance in the heat.
509	
510	                           6.2. Caffeine Supplementation for Exercise Performance in the Heat
511	                                 The meta-analysis of Naulleau and colleagues [92] concluded that consuming 6 mg·kg−1
512	                           of caffeine, ~1 h prior to exertional-heat stress may improve exercise performance; however,
513	                           performance changes were deemed insignificant. Furthermore, the majority of included
514	                           studies showed modest increases in Tc during exercise following caffeine supplementa-
515	                           tion compared to placebo groups [93]. Initial field studies in this area demonstrated that
516	                           caffeine had no benefits on endurance exercise performance when tested in hot environ-
517	                           ments (Table 2 [94,95]). Similarly, the first laboratory-based study to assess caffeine’s effect
518	                           on acute exertional-heat stress identified no improvement in endurance exercise perfor-
519	                           mance [87]. Studies showing no ergogenic effect of caffeine on exercise performance in the
520	                           heat (Table 2 [87,96,97]) have attributed the lack of findings to the potential role of caffeine
521	                           on neurotransmitters, where an increase in noradrenaline secretion may diminish ergogenic
522	                           effects [97]. Additionally, Hanson and colleagues [96] demonstrated increased rates of
523	                           heat storage following caffeine ingestion, even in the absence of performance improve-
524	                           ments. This has direct implications for EHI/EHS susceptibility; however, further research
525	                           using dopamine reuptake inhibitors is required to fully elucidate the effects of varying
526	                           caffeine dosages on neurotransmitter bioavailability and subsequent thermoregulatory
527	                           responses [96].
528	                                 The majority of studies showing no ergogenic effect of caffeine for exercise in the heat
529	                           have only examined cycling-based performance measures [87,96,97]). As caffeine likely
530	                           improves endurance exercise through CNS-related mechanisms, factors such as central
531	                           fatigue are considered more critical performance-limiting factors in endurance running
532	                           compared to cycling [98]. Therefore, running test protocols are likely more appropriate
533	                           for detecting the potential endurance-enhancing effect of caffeine in hot environments. In
534	                           relation, Ping et al. [99] demonstrated improvements in endurance running performance in
535	                           the heat following 5 mg·kg−1 of caffeine administration (Table 2). Although performance
536	                           benefits were observed (31.6% increase in time-to-exhaustion), the subjects were heat
537	                           acclimated individuals; thus, the benefits of caffeine on exertional-heat stress may only be
538	                           observed when individuals previously undergo chronic heat adaptation [99]. Overall, it
539	                           is difficult to truly assess the effect of caffeine on exertional-heat stress due to conflicting
540	                           results across studies investigating differing performance measures, supplementation doses,
541	                           and participants with varying acclimation/acclimatisation status [93]. Additionally, there
542	 Nutrients 2024, 16, 3792                                                                                           11 of 25
543	
544	
545	
546	                           are prominent interindividual differences in caffeine metabolism at the genetic level [100].
547	                           Individuals with homozygous A/A alleles are categorised as rapid caffeine metabolisers,
548	                           whereas C allele carriers (A/C and C/C) are known to be slow metabolisers of caffeine [100].
549	                           As genetic polymorphisms regarding caffeine metabolism are often overlooked in studies,
550	                           it is difficult to propose robust conclusions on the effect of acute caffeine ingestion on
551	                           exertional-heat stress, in addition to providing suggested doses. This is due to the differing
552	                           rates of caffeine metabolism between participants, with acute prescription of the ergogenic
553	                           aid typically administered ~1–2 h prior to exercise performance. Despite this, the major
554	                           consensus regarding caffeine supplementation is that it does not lead to performance
555	                           decrements in the heat; however, observed increases in Tc , HR, and blood lactate warrant
556	                           careful consideration on its use in competitive settings.
557	
558	                           7. Nitrate
559	                           7.1. Mechanism of Action
560	                              Another ergogenic aid that may improve exercise in the heat is nitrate (NO3 − ) [101].
561	                              −
562	                           NO3 is a signalling molecule required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO), a primary
563	                           regulator of arterial pressure [102]. Additionally, NO can be catalysed via redox reactions
564	                           by NO synthase, which can also degrade L-arginine to produce NO. These downstream
565	                           signalling cascades facilitate the vasodilation of blood vessels and increase blood flow to the
566	                           working musculature, subsequently lowering blood pressure [103]. NO3 − supplementation
567	                           is also thought to improve mitochondrial coupling efficiency, which may increase ATP
568	                           resynthesis and enhance exercise capacity [104]. Although the mechanisms are not fully
569	                           elucidated, nitrate also has the potential to improve aspects of cognitive function via
570	                           increased perfusion to the brain [105].
571	
572	                           7.2. Nitrate Supplementation for Exercise in the Heat
573	                                 As mentioned, most studies examining ergogenic effects on performance and health
574	                           are primarily conducted in temperate environments [106,107]. In such environments, pre-
575	                           exercise consumption of NO3 − (300–1050 mg, 2–3 h before exercise [108]) has improved
576	                           performance during sub- and supra-maximal intensity endurance exercise [106,107,109,110],
577	                           and repeated sprint running [111]. This has been attributed to reductions in ATP cost dur-
578	                           ing muscular contractions and reduced oxygen uptake requirements for mitochondrial ATP
579	                           resynthesis [112]. Furthermore, NO3 − has increased vascular conductance and reduced
580	                           blood pressure following beetroot supplementation (~9.2 mmol·L−1 ) in response to locally
581	                           administered thermal skin stimuli [102]. Therefore, it is surprising that previous studies
582	                           investigating the effects of dietary NO3 − on exertional-heat stress have shown no improve-
583	                           ments in performance or thermoregulatory responses (Table 2 [113–117]). However, it is
584	                           important to note that the source and relative quantity of nitrates within beetroot supple-
585	                           ments are highly variable, which can cause discrepancies in findings amongst studies [114].
586	                           Initial research demonstrated that 6 days of nitrate-rich beetroot juice (8.4 mmol·L−1 ) re-
587	                           duced oxygen consumption and increased Tc during the latter stages of a 45 min march in
588	                           the heat [113]. Likewise, McQuillan and colleagues [116] identified that short-term NO3 −
589	                           supplementation (8.0 mmol·L−1 for 3 days) increased Tc throughout low- to moderate-
590	                           intensity cycling exercise in the heat, in addition to offering no further benefit to time-trial
591	                           performance. As blood flow distribution is altered under heat stress to maintain thermal
592	                           homeostasis, increases in Tc may be a direct consequence of NO3 − supplementation. NO3 −
593	                           is suggested to alter blood flow by enabling whole-body vasodilation and overriding the
594	                           homeostatic response to exertional-heat stress [110]. Ultimately, NO3 − may increase the
595	                           rates of hyperthermia development and hinder thermoregulatory mechanisms.
596	                                 The absence of a positive change in performance from nitrate supplementation through-
597	                           out studies may be due to inconsistencies in adopted research designs, sub-optimal con-
598	                           ditions for evaporative cooling, supplementation method, or incomplete analyses of ther-
599	                           moregulatory processes [102]. For example, the NO pathway is potentially initiated more
600	                           efficiently at higher exercise intensities; therefore, the lower continuous exercise intensities

Acute Responses and Chronic Adaptations to Exertional-Heat
Exposure: A Narrative Review
Ryan A. Dunn 1 , Grant M. Tinsley 1 , Ty B. Palmer 1 , Courteney L. Benjamin 2                            and Yasuki Sekiguchi 1, *

                                         Abstract: Global warming is attributed to an increased frequency of high ambient temperatures and
                                         humidity, elevating the prevalence of high-temperature-related illness and death. Evidence over
                                         recent decades highlights that tailored nutritional strategies are essential to improve performance
                                         and optimise health during acute and chronic exertional-heat exposure. Therefore, the purpose of
                                         this review is to discuss the efficacy of various nutritional strategies and ergogenic aids on responses
                                         during and following acute and chronic exertional-heat exposure. An outline is provided surround-
                                         ing the application of various nutritional practices (e.g., carbohydrate loading, fluid replacement
                                         strategies) and ergogenic aids (e.g., caffeine, creatine, nitrate, tyrosine) to improve physiological,
                                         cognitive, and recovery responses to acute exertional-heat exposure. Additionally, this review will
                                         evaluate if the magnitude and time course of chronic heat adaptations can be modified with tai-
                                         lored supplementation practices. This review highlights that there is robust evidence for the use
                                         of certain ergogenic aids and nutritional strategies to improve performance and health outcomes
                                         during exertional-heat exposure. However, equivocal findings across studies appear dependent on
                                         factors such as exercise testing modality, duration, and intensity; outcome measures in relation to
                                         the ergogenic aid’s proposed mechanism of action; and sex-specific responses. Collectively, this

                           particularly problematic for cardiovascular function when performing physical activities in
                           the heat, in addition to exacerbating complications arising from various common health
                           conditions (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes). Despite difficulties quantifying the
                           prevalence of EHI/EHS due to inconsistencies in terminology and criteria for diagnosis,
                           endurance sports and military populations experience the highest rates of heat-related
                           illnesses globally, with ~674.0 cases of EHI per 10,000 athlete-exposures [10]. Therefore,
                           exercise performance in the heat can be suboptimal, with tailored heat mitigation and
                           nutritional strategies required to attenuate heat-mediated decrements in performance and
                           health [3].
                                 Heat mitigation strategies such as heat acclimation/acclimatisation (HA/HAs) lessen
                           the magnitude of physiological, thermoregulatory, and perceptual strain associated with
                           exertional-heat stress [11,12]. These include body fluid and electrolyte losses, increased
                           core temperature (Tc ) and heart rate (HR), augmented substrate utilisation, and enhanced
                           thermal discomfort [13,14]. HA/HAs (involving artificial or natural heat exposures, respect-
                           fully) deliver regular and controlled disturbances to thermal homeostasis [11], inducing
                           chemical, functional, and genetic adaptations that contribute to attaining a thermotoler-
                           ant phenotype [12]. Collectively, these adaptations have been shown to benefit exercise
                           performance in the heat by reducing physiological, thermoregulatory, and cellular stress
                           responses during future exertional-heat exposures [9].
                                 Although chronic heat adaptation strategies procure the most robust adaptations
                           for optimal performance in the heat, singular heat exposure bouts may also improve
                           some aspects of exercise performance in a timelier manner [15]. Acute heat stress typically
                           hinders exercise performance by augmenting Tc , HR, and substrate utilisation [16]. Despite
                           this, Ball [17] highlights the positive implications of acute heat exposure, where elevated
                           muscle temperature-related improvements in metabolic and contractile functioning increase
                           adenosine triphosphate (ATP) turnover rates. Although the effects of acute heat exposure
                           on exercise performance likely depend on the modality, duration, and metabolic demand
                           of exercise, a bout of muscle-damaging exercise in the heat was attributed to reduced
                           physiological strain during future exertional-heat stress [18,19]. Additionally, heat shock
                           protein 70/72 expression was diminished prior to and following subsequent exertional-heat
                           stress, indicative of a lower magnitude of heat-induced cellular stress [20]. This highlights
                           the potential for acute heat exposure strategies to assist in the acquisition of a thermotolerant
                           phenotype [18–20]. Taken together, tailored acute and chronic heat adaptation methods
                           can potentially enhance exercise performance in the heat. However, it is important to
                           continually develop, evolve, and review these strategies with the aim of maximising
                           adaptation potential [21].
                                 Emerging evidence indicates that nutritional and hydration strategies should com-
                           plement heat adaptation interventions to enhance overall performance and safety under
                           exertional-heat stress [22]. Therefore, it is important to review the current evidence sur-
                           rounding these strategies to establish the efficacy and practicality of their use for exercise
                           in the heat [23]. Current reviews, global position stands, and consensus statements re-
                           garding nutritional practices to assist with exertional-heat stress have focused on athletes’
                           knowledge and use of heat adaptation and nutritional interventions, fluid and electrolyte re-
                           placement strategies for health and performance, and recovery following heat stress [22–25].
                           However, there is a need to evaluate the effectiveness and application of nutritional strate-
                           gies and ergogenic aids for various exercise settings in the heat. Therefore, the purpose of
                           this narrative review is to (1) discuss how different nutritional practices and ergogenic aids
                           influence responses to acute exertional-heat stress, and (2) discover how adaptations from
                           chronic heat mitigation strategies (e.g., HA/HAs) can be accelerated with the addition of
                           modified nutritional interventions.

                           3. Hydration and Fluid Replacement
                           3.1. Hydration Status and Exertional-Heat Stress
                                Exertional-heat stress presents numerous challenges for health and performance.
                           In relation to hydration status, exercise in the heat elevates metabolic heat production,
                           whereby increases in sweat rate maintain thermal homeostasis via evaporative fluid losses
                           from the skin [26]. If fluid losses are not sufficiently replaced, reductions in total body
                           water and plasma volume (PV ) adversely alter cutaneous blood flow, elevate Tc , and
                           exacerbate cardiovascular responses during exercise [27,28]. Ultimately, this decreases
                           exercise capacity and compromises cardiovascular stability, increasing the susceptibility to
                           EHI/EHS [29]. It is generally accepted that performance impairments occur when fluid
                           losses exceed 2% of body mass [30]. This can be measured by recording the difference
                           between pre- and post-exercise body weight. Additionally, individuals can use urine colour
                           as simple and practical means of evaluating hydration status, with dark coloured urine
                           indicative of potential dehydration. Therefore, specific fluid replacement strategies are
                           essential to commence exercise in a euhydrated state, especially when performed in hot
                           and/or humid environments [31].

                           3.2. Electrolyte Balance and Sodium Loading
                                 Sodium is an essential electrolyte for maintaining fluid and blood volume. However,
                           the majority of commercially available sports beverages contain sodium concentrations
                           that do not match sweat electrolyte losses from exercise, resulting in a negative sodium
                           balance [32]. This was initially demonstrated by Vrijens and Rehrer [33], who showed that
                           the ingestion of a sodium-containing sports beverage decreased plasma sodium and PV
                           relative to pre-exercise following a prolonged, moderate-intensity cycle in the heat (Table 1).
                           The purpose of the lower sodium content in sports beverages is to promote adequate
                           gastric emptying rates, increase beverage palatability, and favour exogenous carbohydrate
                           ingestion, with the aim of delaying glycogen store utilisation [31]. Regardless, most research
                           investigating the efficacy of sodium suggests that it has a direct role in the maintenance
                           and restoration of fluid and electrolyte balance during acute bouts of prolonged, moderate-
                           intensity exercise in the heat, and can minimise associated PV reductions when given the
                           appropriate dose [34,35]. Despite this, the optimal sodium dose to augment performance
                           and health outcomes has yet to be determined.
                                 The magnitude of sodium supplementation required to optimise an acute bout of
                           exercise in the heat is likely dependent on factors such as individual body mass, in addition
                           to exercise modality, duration, and intensity [32]. Hamouti and colleagues [36] identified
                           that water combined with moderate and high levels of sodium (82 and 164 mmol, respec-

                           tively) enhanced PV by ~5%, compared to ingesting water only, during prolonged exercise
                           in the heat. This expansion in PV allowed for the maintenance of cardiac output and stroke
                           volume during exercise, which in turn, led to a 7.4% improvement in cycling power output
                           during a time-trial in the heat [36]. This highlights the potential of appropriate sodium
                           ingestion for providing cardiovascular stability during exertional-heat stress [36].
                                Ingesting high quantities of sodium prior to an acute bout of exercise in the heat
                           (sodium loading) has been suggested as an effective strategy to optimise performance and
                           thermoregulation [37,38]. To test this hypothesis, previous research assessed the effects
                           of consuming 20–40 mg·kg−1 of sodium, 1–2 hrs prior to prolonged exercise in the heat
                           (Table 1 [36,39,40]). This research demonstrated improvements in thermoregulatory re-
                           sponses (lower Tc , increased sweat rate and PV ) [36,39], with acute sodium loading found to
                           be equally or more effective than supplementation over consecutive days [37]. Thus, acute
                           sodium loading may be practically beneficial for those with limited opportunities to ingest
                           adequate sodium concentrations prior to and during exercise in the heat. Although the
                           mechanisms underlying sex-specific responses to sodium consumption are not fully eluci-
                           dated, it should be highlighted that females may better maintain sodium balance compared
                           to males, likely due to heightened sodium sensitivity [38]. Thus, findings related to sodium
                           ingestion for exertional-heat stress in males should in theory extend to female populations,
                           who may potentially exhibit greater benefits due to enhanced sodium sensitivity [38]. Fu-
                           ture research should seek to investigate the dose–response relationship of sodium intake, in
                           addition to sex differences, on physiological and cognitive performance measures during
                           exertional-heat stress.

                           3.3. Chronic Heat Adaptation with Permissive Dehydration
                                Beneficial changes induced by chronic heat adaptation strategies may be influenced
                           by the hydration strategy adopted (i.e., maintained euhydration or dehydration via fluid
                           restriction) [12,41]. Commencing repeated HA sessions in a dehydrated state (fluid loss
                           of ~2–3% of body mass), termed permissive dehydration, may accelerate physiological
                           adaptations due to the interrelationship between heat strain and dehydration [42]. HA
                           undertaken with permissive dehydration can increase plasma vasopressin and aldosterone
                           concentrations, attributed to improved renal water retention and regulation of blood pres-
                           sure during exertional-heat stress [43,44]. Furthermore, research showed that permissive
                           dehydration during a short-term HA protocol (5 days) in trained athletes increased sweat
                           rate and electrolyte retention, expanded PV , and augmented cardiovascular and thermoreg-
                           ulatory adaptations compared to HA sessions with euhydration [45]. These findings have
                           direct implications for HA prescription in exercise settings, with a possible means of accel-
                           erating adaptation time course and lessening the time burden associated with chronic heat
                           adaptation protocols [11].
                                Despite potential positive implications of HA with permissive dehydration, athletes
                           and their support teams should be cautious when adopting this strategy, as purposely
                           being dehydrated prior to exercise in the heat can exacerbate EHI/EHS risk. Further-
                           more, research surrounding HA with permissive dehydration is equivocal, whereby Neal
                           and colleagues [46] concluded that it did not produce superior adaptations compared to
                           sessions conducted with euhydration (Table 1). Likewise, Travers et al. [47] highlighted
                           that HA significantly improved power output during time-trial performance in the heat
                           when sessions were conducted in a euhydrated state (+19 ± 16 Watts; p = 0.02), with
                           exercise performance adaptations diminished when HA sessions were performed with
                           permissive dehydration [47]. Additionally, when thermal strain is matched, the time course
                           and magnitude of HA-induced adaptations are largely unaffected by permissive dehy-
                           dration, compared to maintaining euhydration [47]. From a health perspective, chronic
                           exertional-heat stress with dehydration may be a contributing factor to acute kidney infec-
                           tion and potential chronic kidney disease [47]. The only study to investigate this showed
                           that HA with permissive dehydration offered no further benefit to exercise performance or
                           physiological adaptations; however, no increases in acute kidney infection markers were
